newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU likely to reject proposed BSE sheep tissue ban.
newsitem.headline: EU likely to reject proposed BSE sheep tissue ban.

text.p: Farm ministers are expected to reject next week a proposal to ban tissue from sheep and goats, as well as cattle, most likely to be infected with scrapie or mad cow disease, EU diplomats and officials said on Friday.
Ministers will also receive a progress report from British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg on the fight against mad cow disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
At their meeting on December 19-20, ministers can use a special procedure to throw out the European Commission's proposal by a simple majority of eight member states.

Last week, 12 members of the EU's Standing Veterinary Committee voted against the proposal, saying the measures were economically excessive as their countries were virtually free of scrapie and mad cow disease.
Britain and France voted in favour. Ireland abstained.
The Commission has proposed that the brains, eyes, spinal cord and spleen should be removed from sheep, goats and cattle over 12 months old and kept out of human and animal food.
Since then only Portugal has shifted its stance, saying it will now abstain, diplomats said.
Diplomats said it was unclear if a British BSE report, due on Tuesday, would mention implementation of a selective cull of younger cattle most at risk to BSE.
The cull, which would involve up to 147,000 cattle, was part of an agreement at the European Council in Florence in June for a gradual lifting of a global ban on British beef exports.
The EU Commission imposed the ban in March after the British government triggered consumer panic by disclosing that people could catch BSE from eating infected beef.

The Commission, which has been criticised for acting too slowly, insists that protection of human health and the restoration of consumer confidence in beef and sheepmeat must be given priority. It insists member states should act likewise.
It has refused to make concessions, saying that no country is totally risk-free and national exemptions would distort meat trade in the EU single market.
But special treatment may be granted non-EU countries, such as the United States, Canada and Australia, provided they can satisfy the Commission about the safety of their meat.
BSE is believed to have arisen from sheep scrapie, a similar brain-wasting disease, which can be passed from one animal to another and from ewe to lamb.
But recent British and French research has shown that sheep could catch BSE. Sheep have also been fed on meat and bone meal, which is believed to be a prime cause of BSE.
